Below is a single, consolidated 12‑week postpartum return plan for your client (33 y/o, 4 weeks post uncomplicated C‑section, OB cleared for light activity now — no abs/heavy lifting until 6‑week check). It integrates phased exercise (strength, core, cardio, progressive HIIT introduction), nutrition for breastfeeding, recovery guidance, progression criteria and red flags. Use clinical judgement and stop or regress for any pain, wound issues, coning/bulging, leaking, heavy bleeding or pelvic heaviness. Consider referral to pelvic‑health physiotherapy if any pelvic floor, diastasis recti (DR) or prolapse concerns arise.

Quick summary of phases and goals
- Phase 0 (Weeks 1–2 of plan; postpartum wk 4–5): Reconnect & Protect — gentle walking, diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic‑floor awareness, light mobility. No abdominal loading.
- Phase 1 (Weeks 3–4 of plan; postpartum wk 6–7): Rebuild Foundation — post‑6‑week check begin low‑load strength, core re‑education (TVA), gentle upper/lower work.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8 of plan; postpartum wk 8–11): Strength & Endurance — increase volume, single‑leg work, introduce light external load and low‑impact intervals.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12 of plan; postpartum wk 12–15/16): Return to Functional Strength & Higher Intensity — 3–4 sessions/week, push intensity safely so she feels stronger by week 12; add HIIT (low‑impact to begin) if pelvic health criteria met.

Program frequency overview
- Strength: 3 sessions/week throughout, progressing from activation to heavier compound lifts and carries.
- Cardio: Daily walking early, progressing to 3 sessions/week (steady + intervals) by Phase 3. Long recovery walks weekly.
- HIIT: Not before ~week 10–12; conservative low‑impact HIIT introduced at ~week 12 if cleared and pelvic floor/core checks pass.
- Core: Gentle TVA work from now, low‑load core exercises starting after 6‑week check, progressing to planks and loaded anti‑rotation work between weeks 8–12 and beyond if symptom‑free.
- Optional 4th session in Phase 3 for accessory work/active recovery.

Safety prerequisites before progressing intensity
- OB clearance for increased activity (especially at 6 weeks and again before heavy/HIIT work).
- Incision healed and pain free.
- No coning/doming at midline during exertion.
- No new/worse urinary leakage, pelvic heaviness or prolapse symptoms.
- Pelvic floor function adequate — consult pelvic physio if in doubt.

Detailed week‑by‑week plan

Plan Week 1 (postpartum wk 4) — Reconnect & Protect
Focus: gentle cardiovascular, breathing, mobility, activation. Home, mat.

3 short sessions (approx 20–30 min) + short walks daily
Session A
- Walk 8–12 min easy (RPE 2–3).
- Diaphragmatic breathing with gentle pelvic floor lift: 3 sets × 6 breaths.
- Supine pelvic tilts: 2 × 8–10.
- Wall push‑ups: 2 × 8–10.
Session B
- Walk 8–12 min.
- Heel slides (small range): 2 × 8 each side.
- Mini bridges (isometric, small range): 2 × 6–8.
- Seated scapular squeezes: 2 × 10.
Session C
- Walk 10–15 min.
- Cat–cow: 2 × 8–10.
- Side‑lying clams (small range): 2 × 10–12 each side.
- Standing balance 2 × 10–20 sec each leg.

Nutrition basics
- Continue nutrient dense diet; prioritize protein (~1.1–1.3 g/kg/day), ~+450 kcal/day above baseline for exclusive breastfeeding (individualize), hydration ~2.7 L/day. Small frequent meals and snacks.

Red flags: stop and consult OB/physio for increased incision pain, heavy bleeding, coning, incontinence, dizziness.

Plan Week 2 (postpartum wk 5) — Reconnect continuity
- Similar to Week 1; increase walks to 12–20 min as tolerated; maintain breathing and activation work. No abdominal loading.

Plan Week 3 (postpartum wk 6) — Begin low‑load strength only after 6‑week check
Prerequisite: OB clearance at 6‑week check.
Frequency: 3 sessions/week, 25–35 min + walking 3–5x/week.

Session 1 (Lower emphasis)
- Warm‑up 5–8 min walk + breathing.
- Glute bridge (supine) 2 × 8–12 (small ROM → increase as tolerated).
- Supported split squat to chair 2 × 8 each leg.
- Standing hip abduction 2 × 12 each.
- Calf raises 2 × 12–15.

Session 2 (Upper + core re‑education)
- Wall/countertop push‑ups 2–3 × 8–12.
- Towel/band rows 2 × 10–12.
- Bird‑dog 2 × 8 each side.
- Dead bug (shallow range) 2 × 6–8 each side (stop for doming).

Session 3 (Mobility + light balance)
- Walk 15–20 min.
- Chair sit‑to‑stand 2 × 10.
- Step‑ups low step 2 × 8 each leg.
- Farmer carry light (milk jug) 2 × 30–45 sec.

Nutrition & recovery
- Emphasize protein at meals and iron‑rich foods for postpartum healing. Scar mobility only when OB allows.

Plan Week 4 (postpartum wk 7) — Consolidate foundation
- Increase sets to 3 for tolerated exercises, slightly longer walks (20–25 min). Maintain pelvic floor and breath sequencing. Begin small range single‑leg control (supported RDL) if incision comfortable.

Plan Week 5 (postpartum wk 8) — Start building volume and single‑leg control

Session A (Lower strength)

- Single‑leg RDL (bodyweight) 3 × 8 each.

Session B (Upper strength)

When to start any abdominal work

  - No new or worsening urinary leakage, heaviness, or pelvic organ prolapse symptoms,
  - She feels comfortable and not lightheaded or dizzy when exercising.
- Progress more intensive abdominal and loaded core work only once pelvic floor strength and diastasis status are acceptable (typically between 8–12 weeks for many women, but individualized).

How to assess readiness (quick tests to perform before adding/titrating core exercises)
1) Incision & pain check: healed wound, no sharp/tugging pain with palpation or movement.
2) Diastasis Recti (DR) basic check (trained professional can do more accurate assessment):
   - Lie supine with knees bent and head lifted slightly into a small curl. Place fingers just above, at, and below the belly button and feel for gap and depth.
   - Look for bulging/coning when she lifts head/does light curl — coning or a gap >2 fingers with a deep separation suggests progress should be conservative and supervised.
3) Functional breath + pelvic floor test: can she perform diaphragmatic breath with a gentle coordinated pelvic floor lift (no bearing down) and maintain neutral spine?
4) Basic load tolerance: can she perform a 2–3 second glute bridge, a controlled heel slide and a supported bird‑dog without bulging or leakage?
If she passes these checks (no bulging, incision OK, pelvic floor coordinated), progress to low load core re‑education after 6 weeks. If not, continue pelvic floor and breathing work and refer to pelvic physiotherapy.

Progression ladder for abdominal/core recovery
Phase 0 — Foundational (Safe now; ongoing)
- Goals: diaphragm‑pelvic floor coordination, avoid intra‑abdominal pressure spikes.
- Exercises:
  - Diaphragmatic breathing with gentle pelvic floor lift (3 sets of 6 breaths).
  - Seated or supine ribcage‑to‑pelvis connection cues.
  - Pelvic tilts and supine heel slides (small range).
- Regress if pain or coning.

Phase 1 — Core re‑education (Begin after 6‑week clearance if checks pass)
- Goals: activate transverse abdominis (TVA) and obliques without flexion/extension or heavy intra‑abdominal pressure.
- Exercises (2–3x/week; 1–2 sets to start):
  - Supine TVA draw‑in (gentle “belly button to spine” on exhale) 8–10 reps — hold 3–5 sec.
  - Toe taps (dead‑bug prep; small range): 6–8 each side.
  - Bird‑dog (slow, limit lumbar movement): 6–8 each side.
  - Heel slides with TVA cue: 8–10 reps.
- Progress when she completes these symptom‑free for 2 weeks: increase sets to 2–3 and add range.

Phase 2 — Controlled dynamic core (Typical start ~8 weeks if symptom‑free)
- Goals: build endurance and control through a fuller range, introduce anti‑flexion & anti‑rotation.
- Exercises (3x/week; 2–3 sets):
  - Dead bug (full range): 8–10 each side.
  - Modified plank (knees) with TVA engaged: 10–20 sec holds progressing by 5–10 sec increments.
  - Side plank (knees supported): 10–20 sec each side.
  - Pallof press (towel or band anti‑rotation) 8–12 each side — focus on bracing, not breath holding.
  - Glute bridges with core bracing: 10–15 reps.
- Progress by increasing hold time, reps, or adding slow limb movements during planks (e.g., heel taps).

Phase 3 — Strength & functional core (Typical start 10–12+ weeks if all ok)
- Goals: add load, more challenging anti‑rotation/anti‑extension, integration with compound lifts and carries.
- Exercises (3x/week within strength sessions; 3 sets):
  - Full plank (progressing to 30–60 sec) if no bulging.
  - Pallof press with increased resistance (timed holds or slow reps).
  - Suitcase carries and farmer carries with increased weight (start light and build).
  - Dead bug to single‑leg bridge transitions.
  - Russian twists with light load only if no doming (controlled, small amplitude).
  - Farmer carry + single‑leg balance challenges.
- Introduce loaded compound lifts (goblet squats, hip thrusts, split squats) with core bracing and breathing technique.

Phase 4 — Power & higher‑load core (After 12+ weeks if all criteria met)
- Goals: return to higher intensity/impact and full core function.
- Exercises:
  - Heavy carries, loaded squats and deadlifts with proper bracing.
  - Short, low‑impact plyometrics (jump prep) if pelvic floor responds well.
  - Rotational medicine ball throws (if available) and higher velocity core drills — only once pelvic floor and DR stable.
- Continue ongoing monitoring for leakage, bulging or pelvic heaviness.

Coaching cues and breathing strategy (always)
- Cue: inhale to prepare, expand ribs laterally; exhale while gently drawing the lower belly toward the spine and lightly lifting the pelvic floor (not hard bearing down).
- On exertion (press, lift, carry), exhale during the hardest phase and maintain a gentle brace, not a hard Valsalva.
- Avoid breath holding. Encourage rhythmic breathing during sets and between reps.
- Teach her to check visually during exercises: no bulging, doming or visible coning at the linea alba.

Examples of safe progression sequences (specific exercises)
- Dead bug progression: toe taps (small range) → heel slides with TVA cue → alternating full dead bug (arms + opposite leg) → dead bug with band resistance (light) → moving to anti‑extension plank variations.
- Plank progression: abdominal hollowing supine → prone on elbows with knees down 10–15 sec → prone on elbows full plank 20–30 sec → plank with alternating shoulder taps (knees then full) → add leg lift or weighted carry exercises.
- Anti‑rotation progression: band/towel Pallof press (isometric hold) → Pallof press with slow pressouts → Pallof rotation with controlled tempo → Pallof holds while performing squats or lunges.

When to stop or refer
- Stop and regress if any of the following occur during or after abdominal work:
  - Visible bulging/coning at linea alba or through incision,
  - New or worse urinary incontinence, urgency, or fecal leakage,
  - Pelvic heaviness or sensation of prolapse,
  - New or increased incision pain or wound issues,
  - Dizziness, faintness, or severe pain.
- If symptoms appear, revert to diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor re‑education and low‑load hip/glute work. Refer to pelvic floor physiotherapist for tailored rehab and diastasis management.

Practical timeline summary
- 4–6 weeks: only breathing and very gentle TVA awareness (what she’s already doing).
- 6 weeks (after OB clearance): begin low‑load core re‑education (dead bug prep, bird‑dog, heel slides).
- 8–10 weeks: progress to planks (knees → full), dead bug full range, Pallof presses, standing anti‑rotation exercises if no doming.
- 10–12+ weeks: add load to core and compound lifts, carries, and prepare for higher intensity/impact tasks if pelvic floor and DR are stable.
- Individual variation is large — progress based on symptoms and functional tests, not strict weeks.

- Weekly total: 120–180 min of mixed cardio (including walks), depending on tolerance.
Session templates (integrate with strength days)
- Steady moderate session (interval/tempo): 30–40 min at RPE 4–5. Example: 5 min warm‑up walk, 20–30 min steady brisk walk or continuous step‑ups on a safe step, 5 min cooldown.
- Low‑impact interval session (higher intensity): 20–30 min total. Example:
  - Warm‑up 5 min easy
  - Intervals: 6–8 rounds of 1 min brisk power walk/march on spot RPE 6–7 / 1.5–2 min easy recovery RPE 2–3
  - Cooldown 3–5 min
  Use incline on hills, fast marching with high knees, or quick step‑ups instead of running.
- Conditioning + power day (per earlier strength plan): Combine 15–20 min of intervals with strength circuit (shorter rest). Example circuit 3 rounds of 8 goblet squats (explosive up), 10 step‑ups, 30 sec farmer carry with 60–90 sec rest — total session 40–50 min.
- Long recovery walk: 40–60 min easy pace once weekly for endurance and active recovery (RPE 2–3).

Progressions and intensity increases
- Increase duration before intensity. If she feels good with 30–40 min steady walks, add intervals the next week.
- Progress interval intensity by increasing the fast interval RPE (from 5–6 up to 7–8) or by shortening recovery times.
- Increase rounds of intervals or duration of steady sessions gradually (10% rule applied loosely to duration/volume).
- Introduce low‑impact plyometrics only in later weeks and only if pelvic floor stable (e.g., week 11–12 mini double‑leg hops or small box hops for 3 sets of 6–8) — monitor for leakage.

- On heavier strength days (lower or upper heavy), do a short 10–15 min light cardio warm‑up (walking, brisk march) before lifting.
- For conditioning days, pair with lighter strength or mobility work — avoid doing heavy strength and intensive cardio on the same day early in Phase D unless recovery is adequate.
- If doing both in one day: do strength first (when fresh), then finish with a 12–20 min interval or steady walk. Keep total session time and fatigue in check.

Breastfeeding, fueling and timing considerations
- Aim to work out ~1–2 hours after a feed/pump to reduce breast fullness discomfort. If breasts are full, she may pump briefly before exercising.
- Bring a snack or have a quick carb/protein source ready after workouts (e.g., banana + yogurt, protein shake, peanut butter toast).
- Increase water intake before and after workouts. Monitor baby’s output and weight if very large changes in training or diet occur (consult lactation consultant if concerned).
- Avoid aggressive calorie deficits; maintain adequate intake to support milk supply and recovery (see the nutrition plan included earlier).

Monitoring and when to scale back
- Scale back intensity/duration if she experiences:
  - Increased bleeding or return of gushes,
  - New or worsening pelvic floor symptoms (leakage, heaviness),
  - Coning/doming during or after activity,
  - Significant fatigue affecting baby care or mood,
  - Dizziness/lightheadedness.
- Return to lower‑impact steady walking and pelvic floor/breathing work for 1–2 weeks, then reattempt progression more gradually. Refer to pelvic physio if pelvic symptoms persist.

High‑intensity interval training (HIIT) can be an efficient way to regain fitness, but after a C‑section it needs careful timing and gradual introduction because HIIT raises intra‑abdominal pressure, can stress the pelvic floor, and is metabolically demanding while breastfeeding. Below is a clear, practical guideline for when and how to add HIIT safely for your client — criteria to meet first, a staged progression, sample sessions, breastfeeding/fueling guidance, red flags, and regression steps.

When to consider adding HIIT
- Not before 10–12 weeks postpartum, and only earlier if cleared and monitored by a pelvic health physio/OB with absence of red flags. More commonly appropriate at 12+ weeks for many women.
- She should meet all of the following before starting:
  - OB clearance for higher‑intensity exercise.
  - Incision fully healed and pain free.
  - No visible coning/doming at the linea alba during exertion.
  - No new/worsening urinary leakage, urgency, fecal leakage, pelvic heaviness, or prolapse symptoms.
  - Able to perform full planks, single‑leg RDLs, loaded carries and moderate loads (as per your strength progression) without symptoms.
  - Pelvic floor function adequate — ideally assessed by a pelvic health physiotherapist if any doubt.

Start conservative: prefer low‑impact HIIT first
- Begin with low‑impact intervals (fast walking, marching, step‑ups, bike/elliptical if available) rather than running, bounding or high‑impact plyometrics.
- Use shorter high‑intensity intervals and longer recoveries initially (e.g., 20–30 sec hard / 90–120 sec easy) and lower total work volume.

Staged progression (example timeline)
- Weeks 4–6: No HIIT. Focus on breathing, pelvic floor, walking.
- Weeks 6–10: No true HIIT. Introduce short low‑impact intervals (1–2 min brisk walk / 2–3 min easy) as conditioning if cleared.
- Weeks 10–12: If criteria largely met and no symptoms, introduce very conservative low‑impact HIIT once/week (e.g., 20 min total with short efforts). Continue monitoring.
- Weeks 12–16+: Progress to 1–2 HIIT sessions/week (low‑impact first), then to moderate/high impact later only if pelvic floor and diastasis remain stable and client feels comfortable.

Sample low‑impact HIIT progressions
Phase 1 — Intro low‑impact HIIT (start ~week 10–12 if cleared)
- Frequency: 1x/week
- Duration: 15–20 min total
- Structure: 5 min warm‑up easy walk; 6 rounds of 20–30 sec fast marching/brisk uphill walk (RPE 7–8) / 90–120 sec easy walk (RPE 2–3); 3–5 min cooldown.
- Monitor for leakage, bulging, heaviness.

Phase 2 — Progressed low‑impact HIIT (week 12–14+)
- Frequency: 1–2x/week (nonconsecutive)
- Duration: 20–25 min
- Structure: 5 min warm‑up; 8 rounds of 30–40 sec brisk power walk or step‑ups (RPE 7–8) / 60–90 sec easy; cooldown 5 min.
- Can include short bursts of fast step‑ups or small bounding on soft surface only if pelvic floor tolerates.

Phase 3 — Transition to higher intensity (week 14–16+ if no pelvic symptoms)
- Only with pelvic floor clearance and no DR/prolapse issues.
- Frequency: 1–2x/week
- Options: 
  - Low‑impact bike/elliptical intervals: 30 sec hard / 60 sec easy x 10–12.
  - Mixed circuit HIIT (bodyweight/resisted): e.g., 30 sec mountain‑climb variation (slow, controlled with core brace) / 60 sec easy march x 8 rounds.
  - Introduce minimal impact plyo drills (small double‑leg hops) only if pelvic floor strong — 3–4 sets of 6–8 reps, not mixed with full HIIT until tolerated.
- Continue to prioritize breathing/brace technique and avoid breath‑holding.

High‑impact HIIT (running, jumping, high plyometrics)
- Delay until at least 16–20 weeks postpartum and only if:
  - No pelvic floor symptoms during/after low‑impact HIIT and strength sessions,
  - Diastasis recti resolved or stable with no doming during high load,
  - She has worked progressively to higher intensities and has pelvic physiotherapy clearance if needed.
- Introduce running/jumping gradually: short strides, limited volume, progress 10% per week on volume/time.

Session examples (low‑impact HIIT)
Example A — 20‑minute walk‑based HIIT
- Warm‑up: 5 min easy walk
- Work: 8 rounds of 30 sec fast power walk uphill or with high knees (RPE 7)/ 90 sec easy walk
- Cooldown: 5 min easy walk + breathing

Example B — Home circuit low‑impact HIIT (no equipment)
- Warm‑up: 5 min march + mobility
- 8 rounds: 30 sec step‑ups (fast but controlled) / 60–90 sec easy marching in place
- Finish: 5 min cooldown + pelvic floor breathing practice

Example C — Bike/elliptical intervals (if available)
- Warm‑up: 5 min easy pedaling
- 10 rounds: 20–30 sec high cadence/effort (RPE 7–8) / 60 sec easy
- Cooldown: 5 min

Breastfeeding & HIIT considerations
- Schedule HIIT 1–2 hours after feeding or pumping to reduce discomfort from fullness.
- Keep water and a quick snack nearby. Bring a high‑protein + carb snack for post‑workout (e.g., yogurt + banana, protein shake).
- Monitor milk supply: brief increases in exercise typically don’t reduce supply, but aggressive calorie deficits combined with high training load can. Ensure adequate calories and fluids.
- If baby shows changes in behavior or output after mother starts HIIT, consult lactation specialist/pediatrician.

How to monitor tolerance and regress if needed
- Keep a simple log for 2–3 weeks after starting HIIT noting:
  - Any urinary leakage during/after session,
  - Any bulging/coning at midline,
  - Pelvic heaviness or pressure,
  - Increased incisional pain,
  - Changes in mood, energy or milk supply.
- If any of above occurs, stop HIIT and drop back to low‑moderate steady state or re‑build with pelvic floor rehab and reassess with pelvic physio.
- If she feels unusually fatigued or sleep‑deprived, reduce HIIT frequency (limit to once/week) or replace with steady state cardio until recovered.

Progression guidelines (practical)
- Start with 1 low‑impact HIIT/week for 2–4 weeks; if tolerated, add a second session the next month.
- Increase interval intensity or shorten recoveries before adding volume.
- Maintain at least 48 hours between HIIT sessions and heavy strength sessions early on.
- Always pair HIIT progress with adequate nutrition and sleep support for breastfeeding needs.

Red flags (stop HIIT and reassess)
- New or worsening urinary/fecal leakage
- Sensation of pelvic organ prolapse or heaviness
- Visible coning/doming at linea alba during exertion
- Incision pain or reopening
- Orthostatic dizziness, fainting or severe fatigue

Bottom line
- HIIT is possible for postpartum C‑section clients, but wait until at least 10–12 weeks and preferably 12+ weeks with the checks listed above.
- Start with low‑impact, short intervals once/week, monitor pelvic floor/diastasis/incision, and progress slowly (intensity → frequency → impact).
- Coordinate with pelvic health physio if any pelvic floor or diastasis concerns before introducing higher impact or volume.

If you want, I’ll:
- Build 2–3 sample 8–12 minute low‑impact HIIT sessions she can start with at week 12,
- Add these HIIT sessions into the existing week‑by‑week plan for weeks 12–16,
- Or create a monitoring checklist she can use during/after each HIIT session to track symptoms. Which do you want?

Below is a single, consolidated 12‑week postpartum return plan for your client (33 y/o, 4 weeks post uncomplicated C‑section, OB cleared for light activity now — no abs/heavy lifting until 6‑week check). It integrates phased exercise (strength, core, cardio, progressive HIIT introduction), nutrition for breastfeeding, recovery guidance, progression criteria and red flags. Use clinical judgement and stop or regress for any pain, wound issues, coning/bulging, leaking, heavy bleeding or pelvic heaviness. Consider referral to pelvic‑health physiotherapy if any pelvic floor, diastasis recti (DR) or prolapse concerns arise.

Quick summary of phases and goals
- Phase 0 (Weeks 1–2 of plan; postpartum wk 4–5): Reconnect & Protect — gentle walking, diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic‑floor awareness, light mobility. No abdominal loading.
- Phase 1 (Weeks 3–4 of plan; postpartum wk 6–7): Rebuild Foundation — post‑6‑week check begin low‑load strength, core re‑education (TVA), gentle upper/lower work.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8 of plan; postpartum wk 8–11): Strength & Endurance — increase volume, single‑leg work, introduce light external load and low‑impact intervals.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12 of plan; postpartum wk 12–15/16): Return to Functional Strength & Higher Intensity — 3–4 sessions/week, push intensity safely so she feels stronger by week 12; add HIIT (low‑impact to begin) if pelvic health criteria met.

Program frequency overview
- Strength: 3 sessions/week throughout, progressing from activation to heavier compound lifts and carries.
- Cardio: Daily walking early, progressing to 3 sessions/week (steady + intervals) by Phase 3. Long recovery walks weekly.
- HIIT: Not before ~week 10–12; conservative low‑impact HIIT introduced at ~week 12 if cleared and pelvic floor/core checks pass.
- Core: Gentle TVA work from now, low‑load core exercises starting after 6‑week check, progressing to planks and loaded anti‑rotation work between weeks 8–12 and beyond if symptom‑free.
- Optional 4th session in Phase 3 for accessory work/active recovery.

Safety prerequisites before progressing intensity
- OB clearance for increased activity (especially at 6 weeks and again before heavy/HIIT work).
- Incision healed and pain free.
- No coning/doming at midline during exertion.
- No new/worse urinary leakage, pelvic heaviness or prolapse symptoms.
- Pelvic floor function adequate — consult pelvic physio if in doubt.

Detailed week‑by‑week plan

Plan Week 1 (postpartum wk 4) — Reconnect & Protect
Focus: gentle cardiovascular, breathing, mobility, activation. Home, mat.

3 short sessions (approx 20–30 min) + short walks daily
Session A
- Walk 8–12 min easy (RPE 2–3).
- Diaphragmatic breathing with gentle pelvic floor lift: 3 sets × 6 breaths.
- Supine pelvic tilts: 2 × 8–10.
- Wall push‑ups: 2 × 8–10.
Session B
- Walk 8–12 min.
- Heel slides (small range): 2 × 8 each side.
- Mini bridges (isometric, small range): 2 × 6–8.
- Seated scapular squeezes: 2 × 10.
Session C
- Walk 10–15 min.
- Cat–cow: 2 × 8–10.
- Side‑lying clams (small range): 2 × 10–12 each side.
- Standing balance 2 × 10–20 sec each leg.

Nutrition basics
- Continue nutrient dense diet; prioritize protein (~1.1–1.3 g/kg/day), ~+450 kcal/day above baseline for exclusive breastfeeding (individualize), hydration ~2.7 L/day. Small frequent meals and snacks.

Red flags: stop and consult OB/physio for increased incision pain, heavy bleeding, coning, incontinence, dizziness.

Plan Week 2 (postpartum wk 5) — Reconnect continuity
- Similar to Week 1; increase walks to 12–20 min as tolerated; maintain breathing and activation work. No abdominal loading.

Plan Week 3 (postpartum wk 6) — Begin low‑load strength only after 6‑week check
Prerequisite: OB clearance at 6‑week check.
Frequency: 3 sessions/week, 25–35 min + walking 3–5x/week.

Session 1 (Lower emphasis)
- Warm‑up 5–8 min walk + breathing.
- Glute bridge (supine) 2 × 8–12 (small ROM → increase as tolerated).
- Supported split squat to chair 2 × 8 each leg.
- Standing hip abduction 2 × 12 each.
- Calf raises 2 × 12–15.

Session 2 (Upper + core re‑education)
- Wall/countertop push‑ups 2–3 × 8–12.
- Towel/band rows 2 × 10–12.
- Bird‑dog 2 × 8 each side.
- Dead bug (shallow range) 2 × 6–8 each side (stop for doming).

Session 3 (Mobility + light balance)
- Walk 15–20 min.
- Chair sit‑to‑stand 2 × 10.
- Step‑ups low step 2 × 8 each leg.
- Farmer carry light (milk jug) 2 × 30–45 sec.

Nutrition & recovery
- Emphasize protein at meals and iron‑rich foods for postpartum healing. Scar mobility only when OB allows.

Plan Week 4 (postpartum wk 7) — Consolidate foundation
- Increase sets to 3 for tolerated exercises, slightly longer walks (20–25 min). Maintain pelvic floor and breath sequencing. Begin small range single‑leg control (supported RDL) if incision comfortable.

Plan Week 5 (postpartum wk 8) — Start building volume and single‑leg control
Frequency: 3 strength sessions/week, 30–40 min + 3 cardio sessions.

Session A (Lower strength)
- Warm‑up walk 5–8 min.
- Glute bridge progression (longer ROM or light backpack) 3 × 8–10.
- Split squat 3 × 8 each leg.
- Single‑leg RDL (bodyweight) 3 × 8 each.
- Side‑lying clams 3 × 15.

Session B (Upper strength)
- Incline push‑ups 3 × 8–10.
- Bent‑over rows (backpack) 3 × 8–12.
- Shoulder tap plank (knees) 3 × 8 each.
- Dead bug (fuller range if no bulge) 3 × 8 each.

Session C (Conditioning)
- Circuit 2–3 rounds: 10 chair squats, 8 incline push‑ups, 10 step‑ups. Walk 20–30 min brisk once/week.

Cardio
- Steady walk 30–40 min (once/week), interval walk 20–30 min (1.5–2 min brisk / 2–3 min easy).

Nutrition
- Continue adequate calories; add small snack pre/post workout (20–30 g carbs + protein).

Plan Week 6 (postpartum wk 9) — Progress load cautiously; continue core re‑education
- Increase load and sets as tolerated. Add backpack of light weight (1–3 kg) to bridges, squats, and rows if form and pelvic cues are fine.
- Cardio: include 1 low‑impact interval session (20–25 min) if pelvic floor stable.

Plan Week 7 (postpartum wk 10) — Build unilateral strength, increase conditioning
- Progress Bulgarian split squats, hip thrusts (couch), single‑leg RDL with longer ROM. Strength sets 3 × 8–12.
- Introduce Pallof press (towel/band) for anti‑rotation 3 × 8–12 each side.
- Cardio: 1 steady 30–40 min walk, 1 interval session 20–25 min; add light conditioning circuit.

Plan Week 8 (postpartum wk 11) — Consolidate Phase 2
- Continue progressive overload: increase backpack load by small increments (1–2 kg), add tempo changes (3s eccentric).
- Strength sample: goblet squat (backpack) 3 × 8–10; hip thrust 3 × 10–12; rows 3 × 8–12; carry work 3 × 60 sec.
- Cardio: interval walks and one long recovery walk (40–50 min).

Plan Week 9 (postpartum wk 12) — Begin intensified Phase 3 (higher intensity)
Prerequisites checked: incision healed, no doming, pelvic floor OK, cleared for heavier work.
Frequency: 3–4 sessions/week (2 strength days, 1 conditioning/power day; optional 1 accessory recovery).

Week 9 specifics
Day 1 — Lower heavy (45–50 min)
- Warm‑up 8–10 min.
- Goblet squat (backpack) 3 × 8 (3s down, 1s up).
- Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8 each.
- Hip thrust 3 × 10 (2s hold).
- Single‑leg RDL 3 × 8 each.
- Farmer carry 3 × 60 sec.

Day 2 — Upper (40–45 min)
- Incline → kneeling push‑ups 3 × 8–10.
- Bent‑over rows 3 × 8–10.
- Overhead press (bottles) 3 × 8–12.
- Rear delt work 3 × 12.
- Suitcase carry 3 × 45 sec/side.

Day 3 — Conditioning/power (35–45 min)
- Low‑impact intervals: 6 × (1.5 min fast / 1.5 min easy).
- Power circuit 3 rounds: 8 goblet squat pulses, 8 hip thrusts, 10 step‑ups.
- Core: Pallof press 3 × 10 each.

Optional Day 4 — Accessory (30 min)
- Single‑leg glute bridges 3 × 8 each, lateral lunges, light plank holds.

Cardio
- Continue 3 cardio sessions/week: 1 interval, 1 steady, 1 long recovery walk.

Plan Week 10 (postpartum wk 13) — Increase load, density and carry volume
- Increase backpack load by 1–2 kg as tolerated; add extra set to main lifts (4 sets on squats or rows).
- Conditioning: more rounds/shorter rest.
- Consider introducing 1 conservative low‑impact HIIT session (see HIIT guidance) only if all pelvic checks remain clear. Start with 20 min: 6–8 × (20–30 sec hard / 90–120 sec easy) of fast marching/step‑ups.

Nutrition during intensified weeks
- Maintain increased caloric intake for breastfeeding and higher activity (baseline + ~450 kcal for lactation + additional 150–300 kcal for increased training as needed).
- Increase protein to ~1.2–1.6 g/kg/day.
- Hydrate well, snack pre/post workout (protein + carb), ensure iron, iodine, vitamin D and DHA adequacy.

Plan Week 11 (postpartum wk 14) — Density & unilateral overload
- Sessions similar to Week 9–10 but with slightly higher volume/weight and shorter rest.
- Incorporate tempo changes (e.g., 4s eccentric squats), longer carries (75–90 sec), and more single‑leg loading.
- Cardio: 1–2 interval sessions (low‑impact), 1 long walk.

Plan Week 12 (postpartum wk 15/16) — Peak week: feel strong and confident
Goal: consolidate strength gains; slightly taper volume to allow recovery and a strong subjective finish.

Day 1 — Lower heavy (focus on top sets)
- Goblet squat 3–4 × 5–6 (heavier, controlled).
- Bulgarian split squat 3 × 6–8 weighted.
- Hip thrust 3 × 8 heavy-ish.
- Farmer carry 3 × 2 min moderate load.
- Short core work: 2 rounds plank variations 30–45 sec (only if no doming).

Day 2 — Upper heavy
- Push‑ups 3–4 × 6–8 (progressed).
- Bent‑over row 3–4 × 6–8 heavier.
- Overhead press 3 × 6–8.
- Loaded carries 2 × 90 sec.

Day 3 — Confidence circuit & conditioning
- Circuit 3 rounds: 12 goblet squats, 10 incline push‑ups, 12 rows, 10 single‑leg RDLs, 60 sec farmer carry.
- Finish with mobility, diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor check.

Optional Day 4 — Active recovery or mobility.

HIIT note
- If introduced earlier, HIIT should be low‑impact and conservative. Preferably start at week 12+ once cleared and after at least 2–4 weeks of progressive strength without pelvic symptoms. Begin with once/week short sessions (20 min) and progress only if symptom‑free.

Core progression integrated across 12 weeks
- Weeks 1–2: diaphragmatic breathing + pelvic floor awareness.
- Weeks 3–4: heel slides, small dead bug prep, bird‑dog.
- Weeks 5–8: full dead bugs, modified planks (knees), Pallof presses, anti‑rotation stands.
- Weeks 9–12: full planks, loaded Pallof presses, carries, integration of core with compound lifts. Only progress if no coning/doming or pelvic symptoms.

Nutrition summary for breastfeeding support (apply throughout 12 weeks)
- Calories: roughly baseline + ~450 kcal/day for exclusive breastfeeding; add ~150–300 kcal/day during higher training weeks as needed. Avoid aggressive calorie restriction.
- Protein: 1.1–1.6 g/kg/day depending on training load.
- Fluids: at least 2.7 L/day baseline; more around exercise.
- Key micronutrients: iron, vitamin D, iodine, DHA, B12 if vegetarian/vegan. Continue prenatal or postnatal multivitamin as recommended.
- Meal structure: 3 meals + 1–2 snacks; include protein at each meal. Quick snack options for workouts: banana + yogurt, protein shake, peanut butter toast.
- Meal prep tips: batch cook grains/protein, keep portable snacks visible, plan around feeds.

Recovery & sleep
- Prioritize sleep and naps where possible. If sleep is severely limited, reduce training intensity/frequency.
- Schedule heavy sessions after a feed/pump when comfortable.
- Include at least 1–2 rest or active recovery days weekly.
- Scar care: gentle scar massage once cleared by OB; avoid straining incisional area.

Progression criteria and red flags (stop/ regress & refer)
Progress only when:
- She can perform required movements with good form and breath control.
- No coning/doming at linea alba during exertion.
- No new/worse urinary leakage or sensation of pelvic heaviness.
- Incision healed and pain free.

Stop, regress and refer if any of:
- Heavy vaginal bleeding, wound separation, increased incision pain.
- New or worsening urinary/fecal incontinence or urgency.
- Bulging/coning at midline during activity.
- Sensation of pelvic organ prolapse or significant pelvic pain.
- Dizziness, fainting, or severe fatigue affecting infant care.

Practical tools for training delivery
- Use a simple checklist before each session: OB clearance status, incision pain check, pelvic floor symptom check, adequate sleep/hydration, and today’s RPE goal.
- Start each session warm‑up with 5–10 minutes walking + diaphragmatic breathing and end with cooldown + pelvic floor breathing practice.
- Increase load in small steps (backpack +1–2 kg increments) and increase volume before intensity where possible.
- Teach correct baby‑lifting mechanics as functional practice: squat/hinge, hold baby close, avoid twisting.

- I can produce a pocket symptom log / HIIT monitoring checklist for your client to use post-workout.
- If you give me her height, weight and feeding frequency, I can provide specific calorie and macronutrient targets.
